newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Lloyd Webber threat to quit UK ungrounded.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Lloyd Webber threat to quit UK ungrounded.

text.p: Andrew Lloyd Webber, the world's best-paid composer, had threatened to emigrate if the Labour party was elected to run Britain.
With little love lost between Lloyd Webber and many ordinary Britons, a vote for Labour was duly billed as a two-for-one deal by vote-hunting politicians.
Labour lived up to its side of the bargain by clinching a landslide victory in the May 1 election.
But Lloyd Webber is still here.
"More broken Tory (Conservative) promises?" one disgruntled Labour supporter wrote to the Guardian newspaper days after the Labour Party's stunning victory.

Despite being one of Britain's most successful businessmen, Lloyd Webber has never matched his spectacular success at staging shows with the personal popularity Britain usually accords its entertainers.
Some blame an imperious manner and frequent temper tantrums. Others point to his looks, an unsympathetic mix even by British standards, and famous prickliness.

The young Lloyd Webber collected wine and wrote musicals while at school. The grown-up version is said to read tax manuals in bed, although aides now say he would only consider leaving the country if Labour brought in punitive new taxes.
But perhaps more than anything, it is the fact that he has made millions of pounds (dollars) staging syrupy musicals, rejuvenating a form of entertainment that many critics thought best left dead.
"The difference between good music and Lloyd Webber is the difference between Michelangelo and a cement mixer," Master of the Queen's Music Malcolm Williamson once said in a fit of pique.
UNFAZED BY UNPOPULARITY
Whatever lies behind his apparent unpopularity -- he is a favourite butt of British jokes -- Lloyd Webber claims to be unfazed.
"One knows perfectly well there is an element of jealousy, so it's not something to worry about. People like my material so what can you say?" he said.
Like is an understatement. People love his shows and love them time and again, despite the prohibitive cost of theatre tickets from Broadway to Shaftesbury Avenue.
Be it "Cats", "Evita" or "Phantom of the Opera", Lloyd Webber is the real star of every show with his trademark lavish sets, technical wizardry and innovation.
"I don't want to sound arrogant but it's easy for me to understand why my work is successful. It's simply because the standard of musicals being offered is regrettably not good," he said.
He wrote his first musical at the age of six.
By 17, he had finished another nine.
And at the grand old age of 44, he was the 10th richest man in Britain and productions of his shows were running in 30 cities worldwide.
"His taste just happens to coincide with zillions of other people. He's so big that he's made Broadway look parochial," said British critic Mark Steyn.
VAST WEALTH, BUT PROFITS FALLING
His success bought him homes in New York, France, Ireland and London, two theatres and a vast private art collection. His pre-Raphaelite paintings are said to be the finest in private hands.

The Independent on Sunday said he swapped lifestyles every time he married. It said he played family man with Sarah Jane, city gentleman cosseted by servants with Sarah and now country gentleman with Madeleine.
He even bought his first wife and her new husband a house, the paper said.

But the great impresario has fallen on hard times, relatively speaking. In this year's list of Britain's super-rich, Lloyd Webber fell two places to the No. 24 spot with an estimated fortune of 550 million pounds ($892 million).
He still topped the list of entertainment and music millionaires, edging out former Beatle Paul McCartney and easily outperforming David Bowie, Elton John and Mick Jagger.
Profits have fallen at his Really Useful Holdings company and buying a Picasso last year for 18 million pounds ($29 million) had, he admitted, "rather cleaned me out".
So now he is getting rid of goods, even dismantling some of his beloved collections.
His London home is on the market for 15 million pounds ($24 million). He recently donated a vintage Bentley from his car collection to the Conservatives.
And later this month (May 20 and 21), Lloyd Webber will sell off some of his collection of fine wine.

"It is a cellar which includes the stuff of every connoisseur's dream. It is a roll call of the most beautiful, and perhaps the most opulent, wines ever to be created," said Serena Sutcliffe, head of the international wine department at Sotheby's auction house.

More than 18,000 bottles will be sold at an estimated cost of more than two million pounds ($3.2 million). Oenophiles say true wine lovers would never have bought such wholesale quantities of high-quality wine, impossible to consume in a lifetime.
Lloyd Webber now recognises his own weakness.
"One of my larger problems is that I'm an incurable collector," he said. "Wine is alive and I now realise that I've been hogging far too much of it. It is time for a cleanout."
